q: Which three elements are needed to produce sound with the voice?
correct: Air pressure, vibrating vocal folds, and a resonator
distractors: Air pressure, a vibrating hyoid bone, and a resonator
Air pressure, tense false folds, and a wind chest
Lung volume, a vibrating tongue, and a soundboard
explain: The voice is a wind instrument: pressurized air sets a vibrator (the vocal folds) in motion, and the vocal tract acoustically enhances the result as the resonator.

q: A singer inhales and then closes the glottis at the same moment that exhalation begins. Which onset is this?
correct: Coordinated onset
distractors: Glottal onset
Breathy onset
Vocal fry onset
explain: A coordinated onset times exhalation and glottal closure to occur simultaneously.

q: Which onset should be used for most singing, whether the singer wants firm mix-belt closure or a light, airy sound?
correct: Coordinated onset
distractors: Soft glottal onset
Breathy onset
Vocal fry onset
explain: The book says a coordinated onset is appropriate for most singing, including firmer closure for mix belt and lighter closure for an airy sound.

q: A singer inhales, closes the glottis, and then releases just enough tension for the folds to vibrate. Which onset is this?
correct: Glottal onset
distractors: Coordinated onset
Breathy onset
Vocal fry onset
explain: In a glottal onset the folds close before airflow begins, and tension is then eased just enough to produce sound.

q: Which risk is associated with excessive use of hard-glottal onsets over time?
correct: Nodes or polyps from high collision forces between the folds
distractors: Singing sharp because too much air is emitted and the pitch drifts upward
A weaker ability to hold long phrases because the breath is used up too fast
Loss of the singer's formant through dehydration of the surrounding tissue
explain: Hard attacks create high collision forces and friction, similar to coughing, and can lead to nodes or polyps; they also tend to produce harsh tone.

q: Which describes a breathy onset?
correct: Exhaling while the glottis is left open or partly open
distractors: Closing the glottis fully before any air flows
Closing the glottis exactly as exhalation begins
Starting with very relaxed closure and a growl-like sound
explain: A breathy onset occurs when the singer starts to exhale before the vocal folds have closed.

q: Why is a breathy onset generally inefficient?
correct: Excess air escapes, which wastes breath and makes long phrases harder
distractors: Too little air reaches the folds, so they cannot vibrate
The folds slam together, wasting energy as collision force
It lowers the pitch and shortens the vocal folds
explain: Breathy onset emits too much air, which impedes long phrases; it also causes noise and often sharp intonation.

q: Which onset typically combines very relaxed vocal fold closure with high airflow and is used for growls in rock, gospel, and jazz?
correct: Vocal fry onset
distractors: Coordinated onset
Glottal onset
Breathy onset
explain: The vocal fry (growl) onset uses very relaxed closure and may resolve into a clearer tone as closure firms up.

q: What is the easiest way to stop the breath at the end of a phrase without closing the glottis?
correct: Inhale at the end of the phrase
distractors: Close the mouth on the final vowel
Open the glottis while continuing to exhale
Snap the folds shut with a soft glottal
explain: Inhaling at the phrase end is a coordinated release, and the breath is usually needed for the next phrase anyway.

q: Why should singers be conscious of their release technique?
correct: It determines whether a phrase ends cleanly and precisely, without distortion
distractors: It sets the vocal fold length for the next pitch and the required breath pressure
It determines the hydration level of the folds during long phrases and rehearsals
It changes the fundamental frequency of the following note and the vowel formants
explain: Release affects musical precision and sound quality: poor releases add noise or pitch and vowel changes, and ensembles must release together.

q: Which of the following is NOT a semi-occluded vocal tract (SOVT) exercise?
correct: Repeated hard glottal onsets on "Uh"
distractors: Singing through a straw
Lip trills
Singing the voiced consonant [v]
explain: Straw phonation, lip and tongue trills, and [v] or [z] all restrict airflow; the "Uh" exercise is an onset exercise for feeling a glottal onset.

q: What closes the vocal folds again after air pressure has opened them?
correct: A zone of low pressure from air rushing through, plus elastic reversion of the tissue
distractors: Contraction of the posterior cricoarytenoid muscle, which pulls the arytenoids together
Backpressure from the lips and tongue, which pushes the air back down onto the folds and closes them
Tilting of the thyroid cartilage by the cricothyroids, which lengthens and thins the folds
explain: Air passing through the narrowed glottis creates low pressure (the Bernoulli effect) that draws the folds shut, aided by elastic reversion.

q: What happens to vocal fold vibration when a singer is dehydrated?
correct: The mucus coating becomes more viscous, so more breath pressure and effort are needed
distractors: The folds thicken permanently and vibrate more slowly at all pitches, whatever the effort used
The mucus coating thins out, so the folds close too tightly and the tone becomes pressed and bright
The glottis stays open, so every onset becomes glottal and the vibrato speeds up
explain: Dehydration makes the mucus coating more viscous, which makes vibration harder, especially for higher pitches.

q: What effect does contracting the cricothyroid muscles have on the vocal folds?
correct: They tilt the thyroid cartilage, stretching and thinning the folds and raising pitch
distractors: They thicken and slacken the folds, lowering pitch and increasing the closed quotient sharply
They open the glottis for inhalation by rotating the arytenoid cartilages outward
They press the folds tightly together for a belt sound and shorten the vocal tract
explain: Cricothyroid contraction tilts the thyroid cartilage forward, stretching and thinning the folds so they vibrate faster, like thinner violin strings.

q: How do singers control pitch, given that they lack direct conscious control over the muscles that tense and thin the folds?
correct: By forming a clear mental image of the desired sound and then producing it
distractors: By consciously contracting the thyroarytenoid muscles until the desired pitch is reached
By lowering the larynx with the hyoid bone and stretching the vocal tract
By raising breath pressure until the pitch is reached, then easing off the support
explain: The book says pitch and tone are controlled through a mental representation of the sound, pre-tuning the system just before singing.

q: On a scale of firmness of glottal closure from 1 to 7, which level is generally associated with classical/legit singing?
correct: Level 4, moderate closure (flow phonation)
distractors: Level 1, very relaxed closure
Level 3, airy closure
Level 7, very firm closure
explain: Classical/legit production generally uses moderate glottal closure, while breathy sounds are at the relaxed end and heavy belt is at the firm end.

q: What does the "closed quotient" measure?
correct: The percentage of each vibratory cycle during which the vocal folds are closed
distractors: The number of times per second that the folds open and close during one held note
The difference between the first formant and the sung pitch, measured in decibels
The percentage of breath pressure lost through the nose during a sustained vowel
explain: A higher closed quotient generally correlates with firmer closure, more overtones, and a higher dynamic level, though too high a value sounds pressed.

q: Why is auditory feedback limited as a guide for singers judging their own sound?
correct: Bone conduction emphasizes low frequencies, so singers do not hear their own spectral qualities accurately
distractors: Singers hear only the reflected sound and none of the direct sound
Auditory feedback affects only rhythm, not pitch
Hearing one's own voice always causes glottal onsets
explain: Bone conductance emphasizes lower frequencies and some sound heard is reflected, so singers also need teacher feedback and kinesthetic sensation.

q: When is a soft glottal onset deliberately useful?
correct: To make words distinct, as in "her eyes," and to help choral rhythmic precision
distractors: To begin every phrase that starts on a consonant so that the words sound smoother
To create a rough, gritty sound in rock singing and to protect the vocal folds
To raise breath pressure for high pitches and reduce the closed quotient of the folds
explain: A soft glottal improves diction and helps a choir be rhythmically precise; it differs from the harmful hard-glottal onset.

q: Why might an adolescent singer have a breathy onset?
correct: Inability to close the posterior one-third of the vocal folds
distractors: Overuse of the thyroarytenoid muscles, which thickens and shortens the folds
Unconscious head movement during inhalation, which pulls the larynx upward
Using a mouth position that is too narrow, so the tongue blocks the airflow
explain: Adolescents may be unable to close the back third of the folds; onset exercises and SOVT exercises help, but some breathiness remains until maturity.

q: Which straw is generally more effective for SOVT exercises?
correct: A smaller-diameter straw, such as a 2.5 mm coffee stirrer
distractors: A wide-diameter straw, such as one more than 10 mm across at the opening
A very long straw, regardless of its diameter or the singer's lung capacity
A short straw, since length matters more than diameter for the back pressure
explain: Smaller diameters tend to be more effective, and for straws of 2.5 mm or larger, diameter matters more than length.

q: What is the "massage" effect of SOVT exercises, and which kind of exercise produces it more?
correct: Greater variability in closed quotient, produced more by pulsating exercises such as trills
distractors: A reduction in closed quotient, produced more by humming than by any pulsating exercise or trill
A steady closed quotient, produced more by straw phonation than by lip trills or tongue trills
A narrower epilarynx tube, produced more by fingers over the mouth and by constant pressure
explain: Pulsating pressure varies the closed quotient, and pulsating or combination exercises showed double the massage effect of continuous exercises.

q: Why is closing the mouth on a vowel a poor way to release a phrase?
correct: It changes the vowel and may create a perceived pitch change
distractors: It forces the glottis to open and exhale breathily
It raises subglottal pressure sharply
It prevents the singer from inhaling for the next phrase
explain: Closing the mouth alters the vowel (like an unintended diphthong) and movement compromises the vowel sound, altering perceived pitch.

q: Why is humming sometimes questioned as a true SOVT exercise?
correct: Air escapes through the nasal passages, producing low air pressure in the mouth
distractors: It creates pulsating rather than continuous pressure and thus cannot raise oral pressure
It requires the glottis to stay open for airflow, so the folds never actually vibrate
It restricts airflow so much that the vocal folds cannot vibrate at all when humming
explain: Maxfield et al. noted that humming lets air escape through the nose, giving low pressure in the mouth, which questions its SOVT status.

q: What is the suggested order for SOVT exercises?
correct: Start with a small straw and finish with sustained [i] or [u]
distractors: Start with lip trills and finish with a small straw
Start with sustained [i] or [u] and finish with humming
Start with humming and finish with [v] or [z]
explain: Exercises begin with the highest airflow restriction and progress toward the vowels [i] and [u], transferring the support to normal singing.
